Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says there will be no fall legislative session as the new Conservative government gets its bearings in the short window between being sworn in and the holiday season. “Our government has an ambitious agenda, and we want to ensure legislation is properly prepared and receives the debate and consideration it deserves,” Doerkson said in a written statement on Monday (Nov. 16). The B.C. Conservative Party will have a large majority in the legislature when it does convene, after the party won 64 of 93 seats in the Oct. 24 election. Doerkson had left the door open to recalling the legislature for a short session before the end of the year as he seeks to pursue a slate of changes after nine years of NDP government. Conservative MLAs are scheduled to be sworn in on Thursday evening. The premier and cabinet will then be sworn in on Friday, officially taking the reins of the B.C. government. “Ministers will get to work from day one, advancing our priorities and preparing a substantive legislative agenda for the spring,” Doerkson said. The incoming government can accomplish a lot simply by taking administrative control of the various government ministries and by issuing cabinet orders. This could include changes to the Massey Tunnel project. Doerkson has promised to scrap the tunnel and build a bridge instead. The new government could also get started building other infrastructure, like the promised urgent care centres and Surrey women’s and children’s hospital. Other major campaign promises will need to wait, like the promised repeal of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, or alterations to B.C.’s no-fault car insurance rules. These will require legislation.

The film has won other festival awards and is eligible for consideration for the 2027 Oscars.

items.title: [bbc.com] London police open serious sexual offences investigation into David Walliams
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

London’s Metropolitan Police said on Friday, Nov. 13, that it had opened an investigation into allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving David Walliams, the British comedian and children’s author. Police said the new complaints were separate from allegations published by ITV News and The Guardian, but detectives are also reviewing those reports for evidence of offences. The reports accused Walliams of using his celebrity status to pursue young women and girls. One woman alleged he sexually assaulted her when she was 15, and others said he groomed them as teenagers. Walliams denies criminal wrongdoing and says he never abused his position. The Guardian and ITV said they spoke with more than 100 people during their three-year investigation. Police have not publicly detailed the number or circumstances of the new complaints. The force said specialist officers are supporting those who have come forward. Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney urged anyone affected to contact police, regardless of when an alleged offence took place.

items.title: [livescience.com] NASA's Swift telescope burns up after nearly 22 years
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.title: [thestar.com] Supreme Court hears challenge to Canada’s ban on 2,500 firearm types
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada began hearing a challenge Monday to the federal ban on more than 2,500 types of firearms the government classifies as assault-style weapons. The appeal follows two lower-court defeats for gun owners, advocacy groups and businesses challenging cabinet’s authority to prohibit the guns through regulations. The ban includes some firearms used for hunting and sport shooting. The government prohibited 1,500 models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14, in May 2020 and later expanded the list. Federal lawyers argue cabinet acted reasonably to address public-safety risks, while appellants say the regulations exceeded the authority Parliament granted and failed to account for lawful sporting and hunting uses. The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Protesters breach Microsoft’s 78-megawatt Amsterdam data center site
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Protesters breached the construction site of Microsoft’s planned Amsterdam data center Friday, with around 100 people entering the site. Pure Data Centres is developing the facility, which consists of three towers about 85 meters tall with a capacity of 78 megawatts, for Microsoft as its sole tenant. Dutch police said they detained 150 to 200 people, and one officer was slightly injured. AFP reported that construction stopped for the day. Campaigners say the project’s electricity demand could equal that of Amsterdam’s households, a claim not independently established in the reporting, and argue that the development puts pressure on local power and water supplies. Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

Security researchers found that 35,578 of 37,571 web apps built with SpaceXSI’s Grok Build, a chat-based app builder, were accessible without signing in, exposing business and personal information at SpaceXSI and 30 other organizations. SpaceXSI removed 24 apps made by its own staff and X employees; Claroc said other users’ apps remained available and that it had begun contacting affected organizations.

Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

France summoned Iran’s ambassador on Nov. 10 and said it would seek European Union sanctions and consider other responses to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration systems that Paris attributes to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. The October operation affected about 700 French retail sites. Tehran has denied responsibility. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Paris would take measures it considered proportionate to deter further attacks, including steps it would not disclose publicly. items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.
